```{r uk-gear-map-table, echo=FALSE}
                               "Pelagic seine",
                               "Pelagic trawls, Other mobile/passive gears, Unknown"),
  `AER gear category`      = c("Bottom trawl/seine", "Bottom trawl/seine", "Beam trawl",
                               "Dredge", "Gillnet",
                               "Handline/rod", "Pot/trap",
                               "Purse seine",
                               "Other/mixed")
) |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  style_ft(font_size = 9, total_row = FALSE) |>
  flextable::set_caption(caption = tab_nums("uk_gear_map"))
```

## STECF FDI data: limitations and use as gear-splitting key

The STECF Fisheries Dependent Information (FDI) dataset was obtained for the study area and period. Unfortunately, the FDI Landings table is EU-aggregated (no country breakdown), and the Effort and Catches tables suffer from substantial confidentiality suppression in many strata. In addition, the spatial FDI tables were not available on the STECF website at the time of analysis. Therefore, the FDI data has not been used as the main source of the data for the report.

Despite these limitations, the FDI Effort table retains one piece of information not available in the AER data: **gear code at the FAO level** (e.g. OTB, OTT, SSC, SDN, PTB). The AER combines all of these into a single Bottom trawl/seine category, which conflates conventional otter trawl (OTB) with Danish/Scottish seine (SSC/SDN), two gears with very different fishing patterns and fleet compositions. The FDI gear-code information is therefore used to disaggregate the AER Bottom trawl/seine category, as described below.

**Splitting approach.** For each stratum (year, country, vessel length class, division), the share of each gear code within the Bottom trawl/seine total was computed from the FDI Effort table. This proportional split key was then applied to the corresponding AER fishing days, so that the total days in each stratum are conserved exactly. Shares in the FDI strata are rescaled to sum to 1 within each stratum, handling any within-stratum confidentiality suppression transparently although not taking care of any seasonal dynamics.

**Coverage and fallback rules.** FDI data are used for `r aer_split_years_start`–`r aer_years_end` only. Post-`r aer_split_years_start` strata with no FDI coverage (primarily IRL, DNK, and some BEL and DEU strata where FDI reported zero or suppressed days) are assigned a pooled fallback split key derived from the FDI data aggregated across all available years and countries, stratified by vessel length class.

**Limitations.** Countries for which FDI coverage is sparse (IRL, DNK, DEU) receive a pooled fleet-average split that may not reflect their actual gear mix. Results for these countries should be interpreted with caution and are excluded from the figures showing the French and Dutch trends.

## GFW data (spatial effort distribution and concentration)

Fishing activity data were retrieved via the Global Fishing Watch (GFW) API (gfwr v3.0) using the Events endpoint. Vessel metadata (flag state, gear type, gross tonnage) were obtained from the GFW vessel registry (<https://globalfishingwatch.org>; Kroodsma et al., 2018).

Recent publications have shown that the haul-based effort from GFW may not be a reliable indicator for fishing effort for trawl-based gears (Hintzen et al., 2025). Therefore, we define GFW days at sea in this report as vessel-days: for each day, each vessel is assigned to the ICES division in which it spent most of its time, based on the spatial distribution of AIS positions recorded during that day. This definition is therefore a simple presence-day metric. The effort trends derived from GFW data were found to be very different from effort trends in AER (and FDI) data. An important limitation of the GFW data is that vessels below the AIS carriage requirement threshold (typically 15 m LOA, though requirements vary by flag state and fishing area) are systematically under-represented or absent. This means that gears dominated by small inshore vessels, gillnets, pots and traps, handlines, are structurally under-counted relative to larger trawl and seine vessels, which carry AIS as a mandatory requirement. Therefore, the GFW data are used exclusively for the spatial analysis using effort density maps, spatial hotspots, and effort concentration metrics. The GFW spatial analysis covers the full period `r gfw_years_start`–`r max(study_years)`.

**Kernel density estimation of spatial effort distribution**

The spatial distribution of fishing effort was characterised using kernel density estimation (KDE), a standard non-parametric method for converting a set of discrete point locations into a smooth continuous surface representing effort intensity (Silverman, 1986). For each year, fishing event coordinates were projected onto a metric coordinate system (UTM Zone 30N) and a Gaussian kernel with bandwidth σ = `r sigma_all/1000` km was applied across the full study area, and σ = `r sigma_7d/1000` km for the focused analysis of ICES 27.7.D. The narrower bandwidth for 27.7.D resolves finer-scale spatial structure within the eastern Channel. Both bandwidths are fixed across years so that changes in the density surface reflect genuine shifts in fishing distribution rather than smoothing artefacts. Land is excluded from the estimation window. The resulting surface is normalised to a 0–1 scale within each year, making spatial patterns directly comparable across years regardless of differences in total effort; for absolute effort levels, the AER-based effort figures in Section `r sec["effort"]` should be consulted alongside the KDE maps. KDE is widely used in fisheries spatial analysis to identify persistent hotspots, characterise seasonal grounds and detect shifts in fleet distribution over time (Gerritsen & Lordan, 2011; Kroodsma et al., 2018).

**Spatial concentration metrics: Gini coefficient and top-10% cell share**

Two complementary metrics were computed annually for ICES 27.7.D on a regular `r cell_size/1000` km × `r cell_size/1000` km grid to quantify how concentrated fishing effort is in space, rather than simply where it occurs. The Gini coefficient is a well-established inequality measure, originally from economics and widely applied in fisheries spatial analysis (Greenstreet et al., 2009; Eigaard et al., 2017), that summarises the full distribution of effort across all grid cells on a scale from 0 (effort perfectly uniform across all cells) to 1 (all effort in a single cell). Values above approximately 0.7 indicate strong spatial concentration; a rising Gini over time signals progressive compression of effort into fewer areas, which may reflect displacement from previously accessible grounds, regulatory closures or increasing targeting efficiency. The top-10% cell share is a more intuitive companion metric: it expresses what percentage of total annual fishing events falls within the 10% of grid cells that were most intensively fished that year. If effort were uniform this would equal 10%; values of 40–70% are typical in concentrated demersal fisheries. Together the two metrics capture different aspects of concentration, the Gini reflects the shape of the full distribution while the top-10% share highlights the intensity of the most-fished areas, and tracking both annually allows changes in spatial footprint to be detected even when total effort remains stable.

## Literature review approach

The literature review underpinning Section `r sec["lit"]` draws on four categories of sources:

**Scientific literature** was identified through targeted searches of Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar using the terms: *English Channel fisheries*, *Channel demersal fisheries*, *flyshoot*, *Danish seine Channel*, *beam trawl North Sea Channel*, *scallop Pecten maximus Channel*, *seabed disturbance trawl*, *AIS fishing effort*, and combinations thereof. Priority was given to peer-reviewed articles published since 2010, supplemented by earlier foundational studies where relevant (e.g. Eigaard et al. 2016a,b; Depestele et al. 2016).

**ICES working group reports** were sourced from the ICES library (<https://www.ices.dk>), primarily:

-   *Working Group on Celtic Seas Ecoregion* (WGCSE, ICES 2025a): principal source for demersal stocks in the Channel (sole, plaice, whiting, sea bass, monkfish, megrim, mullet) and for the broader ecosystem and fisheries context of 27.7.d/e.
-   *Working Group on the Assessment of Demersal Stocks in the North Sea and Skagerrak* (WGNSSK, ICES 2025c): consulted for stocks with distributions spanning both 27.4.c and the Channel (e.g. plaice, dab, horse mackerel).
-   *Working Group on Widely Distributed Stocks* (WGWIDE, ICES 2025e): responsible for the assessment of mackerel (*Scomber scombrus*) and horse mackerel (*Trachurus trachurus* western stock), both of which can be important bycatch species in the study area.
-   *Working Group on Cephalopod Fisheries and Life History* (WGCEPH, ICES 2025d): consulted for cuttlefish (*Sepia officinalis*) and squid (*Loligo* spp., *Illex* spp.) in the Channel and North Sea. WGCEPH does not produce formal TAC advice but provides the best available science on stock status and drivers of variability.

ICES advice sheets for the relevant stocks were also consulted directly.

**Official statistics and national sources** include the STECF AER (primary quantitative source for this report), Ifremer fleet and stock assessment reports, the UK Marine Management Organisation (MMO) annual sea fisheries statistics, and the Belgian ILVO annual fleet reports. Where possible, the most recent published edition was used.

**Policy and grey literature** includes EU regulation texts, the UK–EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement fisheries annex and parliamentary reports on post-Brexit fisheries.

All quantitative claims made in the literature sections are cross-referenced with the AER and GFW results presented in Section `r sec["results"]`, and discrepancies or gaps are noted where they arise.


# Results

## Landings trends

### AER landings by species during `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`

The overall landings by species in the study area (27.4.c, 27.7.d and 27.7.e) during all the years available in the AER data are shown in the figure below (left: all gears, right: bottom trawl/seine, beam trawl and dredge). Herring, scallops and tangle (seaweed) have the highest landings for all gears. For the selected demersal fisheries in the study area, scallops, shrimp and plaice have the highest landings overall.

```{r aer-landings-top-species, fig.height=6, fig.cap=fig_nums("landings_top20")}
p1 <- aer_landings_summary |>
  filter(country_code %in% report_countries_aer,
         sub_reg      %in% study_divisions_aer) |>
  group_by(species_code, species_name) |>
  summarise(total_t=sum(live_weight_t, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  slice_max(total_t, n=20) |>
  mutate(species_label = paste0(species_name," (",species_code,")"),
         species_label = fct_reorder(species_label, total_t)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=total_t/1000, y=species_label)) +
  geom_col(fill="#4E79A7") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.03))) +
  labs(subtitle = "All gears",
       x="Total landed weight (1000 t)", y="") +
  theme_bw()

p2 <- aer_landings_summary |>
  filter(country_code %in% report_countries_aer,
         sub_reg      %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category %in% capacity_gears) |>
  group_by(species_code, species_name) |>
  summarise(total_t=sum(live_weight_t, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  slice_max(total_t, n=20) |>
  mutate(species_label = paste0(species_name," (",species_code,")"),
         species_label = fct_reorder(species_label, total_t)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=total_t/1000, y=species_label)) +
  geom_col(fill="#4E79A7") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.03))) +
  labs(subtitle = "Selected gears",
       x="Total landed weight (1000 t)", y="") +
  theme_bw()

p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = paste0("AER — Top 20 species by total landed weight  |  ",
                     "Divisions: ", paste(study_divisions_aer, collapse=" & ")),
    caption = paste0("Total landed weight per species, ",
                     aer_years_start, "–", aer_years_end,
                     ". Left: all gears. Right: selected gears only."),
    theme   = theme(
      plot.title   = element_text(size=12, face="bold"),
      plot.caption = element_text(size=8,  colour="grey40")
    )
  )
```

Tangle (LQD) is a seaweed species being harvested from the sea (*Laminaria digitata*). Common European bittersweet (GKL) is a shellfish species (*Glycymeris glycymeris*).

### AER total landed weight by year, country and gear

Total landings by gear and country are shown in the figure below. Highest landings are in the category Other/mixed which includes pelagic trawl (for e.g. herring). Beam trawl, bottom trawl/seine and dredge are the three gear types that generate somewhat comparable amounts of landings. Beam trawl is dominated by the Netherlands and bottom trawl/seine and dredge by France.

```{r aer-landings-total, fig.height=8, fig.cap=fig_nums("landings_gear")}
aer_landings_summary |>
  remove_pelagic_anomaly() |>
  filter(country_code %in% report_countries_aer,
         sub_reg      %in% study_divisions_aer) |>
  group_by(year, country_code, gear_category) |>
  summarise(live_weight_t=sum(live_weight_t, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  complete(year, country_code, gear_category, fill=list(live_weight_t=NA_real_)) |>
  mutate(country_code = factor(country_code, levels=report_countries_aer)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=live_weight_t, colour=country_code)) +

                      name="Country") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(aer_years_start, aer_years_end, by=2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05))) +
  facet_wrap(~gear_category) +
  labs(title   = "AER — Landed weight by gear category",
       subtitle = paste("Divisions:", paste(study_divisions_aer, collapse=" & ")),
       caption  = pelagic_anomaly_note,
       x="Year", y="Landed weight (t)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(strip.text   = element_text(size=7),
        axis.text.x  = element_text(angle=45, hjust=1),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.caption = element_text(size=6.5, colour="grey40"))
```

### AER total landed weight for Other/mixed gear by year, country and species group

The Other/mixed gear category covers a highly diverse range of fishing techniques and target species that do not fit neatly into the main AER gear categories. The composition of this category differs markedly by country. French Other/mixed landings are dominated by seaweeds (tangle LQD and kelp LAH, harvested mechanically from the seabed) and pelagic fish (herring, mackerel, sardine and horse mackerel), together accounting for over 60% of French Other/mixed volume throughout the series. The increase in French Other/mixed landings since 2019, visible in the preceding landings-by-gear figure, is driven largely by growing seaweed harvests rather than increasing pelagic or demersal fishing activity. Dutch Other/mixed landings are almost entirely pelagic fish, consistent with the Dutch pelagic trawl fleet (pair trawlers targeting herring, horse mackerel and mackerel in the Channel), though showing considerable interannual variability linked to stock availability and quota allocation. German Other/mixed landings are a modest but stable contribution, also predominantly pelagic. Belgian Other/mixed landings are negligible at this scale and have been omitted.

```{r aer-landings-species-country-groups, fig.height=5, fig.cap=fig_nums("landings_spp_grp_cty")}
plot_data <- aer_landings_summary |>
  remove_pelagic_anomaly() |>
  filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category == "Other/mixed",
         country_code  %in% report_countries_aer,
         country_code != "BEL",
         year          %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end) |>
  mutate(species_group = assign_species_group(species_code, species_name),
         species_group = if_else(is.na(species_group), "Other", species_group),
         species_group = factor(species_group,
                                levels = c(species_group_levels, "Other"))) |>
  group_by(year, country_code, species_group) |>
  summarise(live_weight_t = sum(live_weight_t, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  complete(year         = aer_years_start:aer_years_end,
           # country_code = report_countries_aer,
           species_group,
           fill = list(live_weight_t = 0)) |>
  # Set 2012 NLD to NA so the bar is fully absent
  mutate(live_weight_t = if_else(
    country_code == "NLD" & year == 2012,
    NA_real_, live_weight_t)) |>
  mutate(country_code = factor(country_code, levels=report_countries_aer))

asterisk_data <- data.frame(
  country_code = factor("NLD", levels=report_countries_aer),
  year         = 2012,
  label        = "*"
)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x=year, y=live_weight_t/1000, fill=species_group)) +
  geom_col(position="stack", width=0.8, na.rm=TRUE) +
  geom_text(data=asterisk_data, aes(x=year, y=0, label=label),
            inherit.aes=FALSE, vjust=-0.3, size=6,
            colour="red", fontface="bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=species_group_colours, name="Species group", drop=FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(aer_years_start, aer_years_end, by=2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05)),
                     labels=scales::label_comma()) +
  facet_wrap(~country_code, ncol=3) +
  labs(title    = "AER — Other/mixed gear: landings by species group and country",
       subtitle = paste0("Divisions: ", paste(study_divisions_aer, collapse=" & "),
                         "  —  ", aer_years_start, "\u2013", aer_years_end),
       caption  = pelagic_anomaly_note,
       x="Year", y="Landed weight (1000 t)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x     = element_text(angle=45, hjust=1),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text      = element_text(face="bold"),
        plot.caption    = element_text(size=6.5, colour="grey40")) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow=3))
```

### AER key species groups: landings by country

Landings in the study area are dominated by flatfishes, scallops and shrimps in terms of volume, with flatfish landings showing a marked decline from around 40,000 t in 2008 to below 15,000 t by 2023, driven almost entirely by the Dutch (NLD) and Belgian (BEL) fleets. This is consistent with the contraction of beam trawl effort over this period. Scallop landings are dominated by France (FRA) and show an increasing trend since 2016, reaching record levels in 2022–2023. Shrimp landings are predominantly Dutch, in the Southern North Sea and relatively stable. Cephalopod landings (cuttlefish and squid) are France-dominated and show moderate interannual variability. Landings of mackerel, horse mackerel, whiting, mullets and gurnards are comparatively low across all countries.

```{r aer-landings-species-country, fig.height=10, fig.cap=fig_nums("landings_spp_cty")}
plot_data_cty <- aer_landings_summary |>
  remove_pelagic_anomaly() |>
  filter(country_code  %in% report_countries_aer,
         sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
         year          <= aer_years_end) |>
  mutate(species_group = assign_species_group(species_code, species_name)) |>
  filter(!is.na(species_group)) |>
  group_by(year, country_code, species_group) |>
  summarise(live_weight_t=sum(live_weight_t, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  complete(year, country_code, species_group, fill=list(live_weight_t=0)) |>
  mutate(country_code  = factor(country_code, levels=report_countries_aer),
         species_group = factor(species_group, levels=species_group_levels)) |>
  # Set entire 2012 Pelagic fish bar to NA — anomaly makes year unreliable
  mutate(live_weight_t = if_else(
    year == 2012 & species_group == "Pelagic fish",
    NA_real_, live_weight_t))

asterisk_cty <- data.frame(
  species_group = factor("Pelagic fish", levels=species_group_levels),
  year          = 2012,
  label         = "*"
)

ggplot(plot_data_cty, aes(x=year, y=live_weight_t, fill=country_code)) +
  geom_col(position="stack", width=0.8, na.rm=TRUE) +
  geom_text(data=asterisk_cty, aes(x=year, y=0, label=label),
            inherit.aes=FALSE, vjust=-0.3, size=5,
            colour="red", fontface="bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=flag_colours, drop=FALSE, na.value="grey70",
                    name="Country") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(aer_years_start, aer_years_end, by=2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05))) +
  facet_wrap(~species_group, ncol=3) +
  labs(title    = "AER — Landings by key species group and country",
       subtitle = paste0("Divisions: ", paste(study_divisions_aer, collapse=" & "),
                         "  —  Gears: ", paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")),
       caption  = paste0("Countries stacked additively.\n", pelagic_anomaly_note),
       x="Year", y="Landed weight (t)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x  = element_text(angle=45, hjust=1),
        strip.text   = element_text(size=7),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.caption = element_text(size=6.5, colour="grey40"))
```

### AER key species groups: landings by gear category

The gear breakdown confirms that flatfish landings are almost entirely taken by beam trawl, with a steep decline since 2008. Scallops are dominated by dredge. Cuttlefish, squid, gurnards and whiting are taken predominantly by bottom trawl/seine. Shrimps are exclusively beam trawl. Mullets, mackerel and horse mackerel show negligible landings across all gears.

```{r aer-landings-species-gear, fig.height=10, fig.cap=fig_nums("landings_spp_gear")}
plot_data_gear <- aer_landings_summary |>
  remove_pelagic_anomaly() |>
  filter(country_code  %in% report_countries_aer,
         sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
         year          <= aer_years_end) |>
  mutate(species_group = assign_species_group(species_code, species_name)) |>
  filter(!is.na(species_group)) |>
  group_by(year, gear_category, species_group) |>
  summarise(live_weight_t=sum(live_weight_t, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  complete(year, gear_category, species_group, fill=list(live_weight_t=0)) |>
  mutate(species_group = factor(species_group, levels=species_group_levels)) |>
  # Set entire 2012 Pelagic fish bar to NA — anomaly makes year unreliable
  mutate(live_weight_t = if_else(
    year == 2012 & species_group == "Pelagic fish",
    NA_real_, live_weight_t))

asterisk_gear <- data.frame(
  species_group = factor("Pelagic fish", levels=species_group_levels),
  year          = 2012,
  label         = "*"
)

ggplot(plot_data_gear, aes(x=year, y=live_weight_t, fill=gear_category)) +
  geom_col(position="stack", width=0.8, na.rm=TRUE) +
  geom_text(data=asterisk_gear, aes(x=year, y=0, label=label),
            inherit.aes=FALSE, vjust=-0.3, size=5,
            colour="red", fontface="bold") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="Set2") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(aer_years_start, aer_years_end, by=2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05))) +
  facet_wrap(~species_group, ncol=3) +
  labs(title    = "AER — Landings by key species group and gear category",
       subtitle = paste0("Divisions: ", paste(study_divisions_aer, collapse=" & "),
                         "  —  Gears: ", paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")),
       caption  = pelagic_anomaly_note,
       x="Year", y="Landed weight (t)", fill="Gear category") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x  = element_text(angle=45, hjust=1),
        strip.text   = element_text(size=7),
        legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.caption = element_text(size=6.5, colour="grey40"))
```

### Including UK landings (`r min(combined_years)`–`r max(combined_years)`)

The figures in Sections `r sec["landings_first"]`–`r sec["landings_last_aer"]` are based on the AER and therefore exclude the UK fleet. To complete the picture of landings in the study area, UK landings from the MMO (Section `r sec["uk"]`) were combined with the AER landings for `r min(combined_years)`–`r max(combined_years)`, the years covered by both sources. Over this period, UK and Channel Islands vessels accounted for `r uk_share_pct`% of total landings in the study area (`r uk_pct_div("27.4.c")`% in 27.4.c, `r uk_pct_div("27.7.d")`% in 27.7.d and `r uk_pct_div("27.7.e")`% in 27.7.e).

```{r landings-eu-uk-country, fig.height=5, fig.cap=fig_nums("landings_eu_uk_country")}
landings_combined_overlap |>
  mutate(country_code = if_else(country_code %in% report_countries_combined,
                                country_code, "Other"),
         country_code = factor(country_code,
                               levels = c(report_countries_combined, "Other"))) |>
  group_by(year, sub_reg, country_code) |>
  summarise(t = sum(live_weight_t, na.rm = TRUE) / 1000, .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = t, fill = country_code)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = flag_colours, drop = FALSE, name = "Country") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = combined_years) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
                     labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  facet_wrap(~sub_reg) +
  labs(title    = "EU (AER) and UK (MMO) landings by division and country",
       subtitle = "All gears",
       caption  = "GBR = UK vessels; CHI = Jersey and Guernsey vessels.",
       x = "Year", y = "Landed weight (1000 t)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.caption    = element_text(size = 6.5, colour = "grey40"))
```

The species composition of the UK landings is dominated by shellfish (whelk, scallops, cockles and crab) together with horse mackerel, flatfish and cuttlefish. Including the UK therefore shifts the overall species composition of the study area towards shellfish and crustaceans.

```{r landings-eu-uk-spp, fig.height=6, fig.width=10, fig.cap=fig_nums("landings_eu_uk_spp")}
spp_cty <- landings_combined_overlap |>
  mutate(species_group = assign_species_group(species_code_harm, species_name_harm),
         species_group = factor(replace_na(species_group, "Other"),
                                levels = c(species_group_levels, "Other")),
         country_code  = if_else(country_code %in% report_countries_combined,
                                 country_code, "Other"),
         country_code  = factor(country_code,
                                levels = c(report_countries_combined, "Other"))) |>
  group_by(country_code, species_group) |>
  summarise(t = sum(live_weight_t, na.rm = TRUE) / length(combined_years) / 1000,
            .groups = "drop") %>% 
  mutate(country_code = fct_reorder(country_code, t, .fun = sum, .desc = TRUE))

p_abs <- ggplot(spp_cty, aes(x = country_code, y = t, fill = species_group)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = species_group_colours, drop = FALSE,
                    name = "Species group") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
                     labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(subtitle = "Absolute", x = "", y = "Average landed weight per year (1000 t)") +
  theme_bw()

p_pct <- ggplot(spp_cty, aes(x = country_code, y = t, fill = species_group)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill", width = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = species_group_colours, drop = FALSE,
                    name = "Species group") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0)),
                     labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(subtitle = "Percentage", x = "", y = "Share of landed weight") +
  theme_bw()

p_abs + p_pct +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Average annual landings by country and species group, EU + UK",
    subtitle = paste0("Divisions: ", paste(study_divisions_aer, collapse = " & "),
                      "  —  ", min(combined_years), "\u2013", max(combined_years),
                      "  —  All gears"),
    theme    = theme(plot.title      = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
                     plot.subtitle   = element_text(size = 9, colour = "grey30"),
                     legend.position = "bottom")
  ) &
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 3))
```

Unlike the AER, the UK data distinguish demersal trawls from demersal seines, so the gear composition of UK landings can be shown directly, without the FDI-based split of Section `r sec["split"]`. The main gears are pots and traps and dredge in the whole study area, and pelagic trawl and demersal seine in 27.7.d and beam trawl in 27.7.e.

```{r landings-uk-gear, fig.height=5, fig.cap=fig_nums("landings_uk_gear")}

       subtitle = "MMO data, original UK gear categories",

  theme_bw() +

        axis.text.x     = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

## Effort trends (STECF AER)

### Total fishing days by year and country (all gears)

Total fishing effort in the study area declined from around 235,000 days in 2008 to approximately 160,000 days in 2023, a reduction of more than 30% over the period. France consistently dominates total effort, accounting for approximately 80% of fishing days throughout the series. The Netherlands is the second largest contributor, with effort relatively stable over the period. Belgian and German effort is small and declining. The overall downward trend is driven primarily by reductions in French effort, with a notable step-down around 2019–2020 that may partly reflect COVID-19 disruption as well as post-Brexit access restrictions in subsequent years.

```{r aer-effort-country-total, fig.height=5, fig.cap=fig_nums("effort_country")}

                              country_code, "Other")) |>
```

### Total fishing days by year, country and gear category

The breakdown of effort by gear category reveals that the dominant gears in the study area are bottom trawl/seine, dredge, gillnet and pot/trap, with the Other/mixed category contributing a substantial and growing share in 27.7.D (see Section `r sec["other_mixed"]` for further analysis of that category). Bottom trawl/seine effort is predominantly French throughout, with a gradual declining trend. Dredge effort is almost exclusively French, reflecting the scallop fleet operating in 27.7.D and 27.7.E. The Dutch fleet is most visible in beam trawl and, to a lesser extent, Other/mixed. Belgian effort appears primarily in beam trawl and shows the strongest decline of any national fleet over the period.

```{r aer-effort-gear-cat, fig.height=8, fig.cap=fig_nums("effort_gear_cat")}
aer_effort_summary |>

         year         <= aer_years_end) |>
  group_by(year, country_code, gear_category) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  complete(year, country_code, gear_category,
           fill = list(totfishdays = NA_real_)) |>
  mutate(country_code = factor(country_code, levels=report_countries_aer)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=totfishdays, colour=country_code)) +
  geom_line(na.rm=TRUE) +

  scale_colour_manual(values=flag_colours, drop=FALSE, na.value="grey70",
                      name="Country") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(aer_years_start, aer_years_end, by=2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05)),

        legend.position = "bottom")
```

### Total fishing days by year, country and vessel length class

Fishing effort by vessel length class reveals distinct fleet structures by country. The French fleet (FRA) dominates across the smaller vessel size classes, with the largest absolute number of fishing days in the smaller vessel classes (VL0010–VL1218). This reflects the broad size distribution of the French demersal fleet. French effort shows a gradual declining trend across most size classes over the period. The Dutch fleet (NLD) is concentrated in the medium-to-large vessel classes (VL1824 and VL40XX), consistent with the flyshoot and beam trawl fleet composition, and shows relatively stable effort over time. Belgian effort (BEL) is most visible in the VL1824 class and shows a clear declining trend, consistent with the contraction of the Belgian beam trawl fleet documented in the landings data. German effort (DEU) is negligible across all size classes. Notably, the VL1824 class shows the most multi-country competition for effort, with French, Dutch and Belgian vessels all active in this size range.

```{r aer-effort-trend, fig.height=6, fig.cap=fig_nums("effort_gear")}
aer_effort_summary |>

  group_by(year, country_code, vessel_length) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  complete(year, country_code, vessel_length, fill=list(totfishdays=NA_real_)) |>
  mutate(country_code  = factor(country_code,  levels=report_countries_aer),
         vessel_length = factor(vessel_length,
                                levels=c("VL0010","VL1012","VL1218",
                                         "VL1824","VL2440","VL40XX"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=totfishdays, colour=country_code)) +
  geom_line(na.rm=TRUE) + geom_point(size=1.5, na.rm=TRUE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=flag_colours, drop=FALSE, na.value="grey70",
                      name="Country") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(aer_years_start, aer_years_end, by=2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05))) +
  facet_wrap(~vessel_length, ncol=3) +
  labs(title    = "AER: Fishing days by vessel length class",
       subtitle = paste0("Divisions: ", paste(study_divisions_aer, collapse=" & "),
                         "  —  Gears: ", paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")),
       x="Year", y="Fishing days", colour="Country") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(strip.text=element_text(size=8), axis.text.x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1),
        legend.position="bottom")
```

### Total fishing days by year and vessel size class (selected gears)

Total effort for selected gears declined from around 120,000 days in 2008 to approximately 75,000 days in 2023. The decline is most pronounced in the medium vessel classes (VL1218 and VL1824), which together historically dominated total effort. Smaller vessels (VL0010–VL1012) show greater stability, while the largest vessels (VL2440–VL40XX) contribute relatively little throughout.

### Fishing days by year, country, gear and vessel size

The figure below reveals clear fleet specialisation by gear and vessel size. French vessels dominate bottom trawl/seine effort across all size classes, with a modest declining trend. Belgian effort is similarly concentrated in beam trawl VL1824, also declining markedly. ### Disaggregation of bottom trawl/seine into OTB and SSC/SDN (FDI-derived)

As described in Section `r sec["fdi"]`, the AER Bottom trawl/seine category was disaggregated into conventional otter trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB) and seine (SSC/SDN) gears using proportional split keys derived from the STECF FDI Effort data. Overall, approximately 57% of Bottom trawl/seine fishing days are attributed to conventional otter trawl (OTB), with seine (SSC/SDN) accounting for around 7–13% and growing modestly over the `r aer_split_years_start`–`r aer_years_end` period. The picture varies strongly by country: France is almost exclusively OTB (~96%), while the Netherlands is predominantly seine (SSC/SDN, ~72%), reflecting the Dutch flyshoot fleet composition. Caveat: BEL and DEU received pooled fallback splits due to sparse FDI coverage.

```{r aer-split-trend, fig.height=5, fig.width=10, fig.cap=fig_nums("split_total")}
if (!is.null(aer_split)) {

  split_2colours <- c(
    "Bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB)" = "#E15759",
    "Seine (SSC/SDN)"             = "#4E79A7"
  )
  
  p_abs <- aer_split |>
    filter(year <= aer_years_end,
           gear_type != "Unsplit") |>
    group_by(year, gear_type) |>
    summarise(fishdays = sum(totfishdays_split, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
    mutate(gear_type = factor(gear_type, levels=names(split_2colours))) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=year, y=fishdays, fill=gear_type)) +
    geom_col(position="stack", width=0.8) +
    scale_fill_manual(values=split_2colours, name=NULL, guide  = guide_legend(nrow=1)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(aer_split_years_start, aer_years_end, by=2)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05)),
                       labels=scales::label_comma()) +
    labs(subtitle="Absolute fishing days", x="Year", y="Fishing days") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(axis.text.x   = element_text(angle=45, hjust=1),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(size=9, colour="grey30"))

p_pct <- aer_split |>
    filter(year         %in% aer_split_years_start:aer_years_end,
           split_source == "FDI direct",
           gear_type    != "Unsplit") |>
    group_by(year, gear_type) |>
    summarise(totdays = sum(totfishdays_split, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
    group_by(year) |>
    mutate(pct = round(100 * totdays / sum(totdays), 0)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(gear_type = factor(gear_type, levels=names(split_2colours))) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=year, y=pct, colour=gear_type, group=gear_type)) +
    geom_line(linewidth=1) +
    geom_point(size=3) +
    geom_text(aes(label=paste0(pct, "%")),
              vjust=-0.8, size=2.8, show.legend=FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values=split_2colours, name=NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(aer_split_years_start, aer_years_end, by=2)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0, 100),
                       expand=expansion(mult=c(0, 0.08)),
                       labels=scales::label_percent(scale=1)) +
    labs(subtitle="Gear share (%) — FDI direct splits only",
         x="Year", y="Share of fishing days (%)") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(legend.position = "none",          # suppress p_pct legend entirely
          axis.text.x     = element_text(angle=45, hjust=1),
          plot.subtitle   = element_text(size=9, colour="grey30"))

p_abs + p_pct +
  plot_layout(guides="collect") +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "AER — Bottom trawl/seine disaggregated by gear code",
    subtitle = paste0("Divisions: ", paste(study_divisions_aer, collapse=" & "),
                      "  —  FDI gear-code split applied to AER fishing days"),
    theme    = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(size=11, face="bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size=9, colour="grey30"),
      legend.position = "bottom"    # set here on the annotation theme, not with &
    )
  )

} else {
  cat("aer_split not available.\n")
}
```

## Global Fishing Watch (GFW) effort data and comparison with AER

### Total GFW fishing days by year and flag state

GFW-derived fishing effort in the study area shows a clear increasing trend from around 53,000 days in 2013 to approximately 90,000 days in 2024–2025, contrasting with the declining trend seen in the AER data. Unlike the AER-based figures, the GFW series includes the United Kingdom (GBR), which accounts for approximately 25–30% of total effort in the area and is the second largest contributor after the Netherlands. The size class breakdown shows that effort is dominated by small vessels (S1 <100 GT), with a growing contribution from this class driving much of the overall increase. French and Dutch effort appears relatively stable in the GFW series, suggesting the overall increase may partly reflect improving AIS coverage over time rather than a genuine increase in fishing activity.

```{r gfw-plot-flag-total, fig.cap=fig_nums("gfw_flag_total")}

                  legend.position = "bottom")
```

### AER vs GFW effort comparison

The two data sources measure effort differently: AER reports administrative fishing days declared by member states; GFW estimates fishing days from AIS vessel-tracking. The comparison below shows total fishing days over the overlapping period `r gfw_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`. Note that the AER series excludes GBR (post-Brexit data are not consistently included in the STECF AER) while the GFW series includes all five countries.

Several factors can explain systematic differences between the two series:

-   **Method for counting fishing days**: AER records one fishing day as any day on which a vessel is registered as fishing by its flag state; GFW counts a vessel-day as active when AIS-derived speed and movement patterns are classified as fishing behaviour. The two methods can disagree for the same vessel on the same day.
-   **AIS coverage and adoption**: AIS was gradually mandated across the EU fleet between 2008 and 2014. Early years of the GFW series therefore under-represent vessels that did not yet carry AIS transponders, leading to lower GFW effort estimates before ~2014.
-   **Small coastal vessels**: Vessels below ~15 m LOA are not required to carry AIS in many jurisdictions. This segment is captured in the AER (via logbook reporting) but largely absent from GFW, causing a structural undercount in GFW relative to AER for gears dominated by small vessels (e.g. pot/trap, gillnet).
-   **Gear type assignment**: GFW classifies gear from AIS movement patterns; misclassification can shift effort between gear categories when comparing with AER gear-specific totals.
-   **Spatial attribution**: AER effort is attributed to the ICES division declared in the logbook; GFW effort is attributed to the GPS position of the fishing event. In boundary areas the two can differ.

```{r aer-gfw-comparison, fig.height=5, fig.cap=fig_nums("aer_gfw_compare")}
# AER: DEU+NLD+BEL+FRA only (GBR excluded — incomplete in AER post-Brexit)
aer_countries_comparison <- c("DEU","NLD","BEL","FRA")
aer_label <- paste0("AER (", paste(aer_countries_comparison, collapse="+"), ")")
gfw_label <- paste0("GFW (", paste(report_countries_gfw, collapse="+"), ")")

aer_total <- aer_effort_summary |>
  filter(country_code %in% aer_countries_comparison,
         sub_reg      %in% study_divisions_aer,
         year %in% intersect(study_years, seq(aer_years_start, 2023))) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(fishing_days=sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  mutate(source=aer_label)

gfw_total <- fishing_days_study %>%
  filter(vessel_flag %in% report_countries_gfw,
         year %in% intersect(study_years, seq(gfw_years_start, 2023))) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(fishing_days=sum(fishing_days), .groups="drop") %>%
  mutate(source=gfw_label)

bind_rows(aer_total, gfw_total) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=fishing_days/1000, colour=source, shape=source)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=1) + geom_point(size=2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=study_years) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.05))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=setNames(c("#E15759","#4E79A7"), c(aer_label, gfw_label))) +
  scale_shape_manual(values=setNames(c(16L, 17L), c(aer_label, gfw_label))) +
  labs(title    = "Effort comparison: AER vs GFW",
       subtitle = paste0("Divisions: ", paste(study_divisions_aer, collapse=" & ")),
       x="Year", y="Fishing days (1000)", colour="Source", shape="Source") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=45, hjust=1), legend.position="bottom")
```

### Spatial distribution of GFW fishing events

The spatial distribution of GFW fishing events reveals clear national zoning patterns across the study area. Dutch (NLD) effort is heavily concentrated in the southern North Sea (27.4.C), particularly around and between the wind farm development zones. French (FRA) effort dominates the eastern and western Channel (27.7.D/E), spread broadly across the division. UK (GBR) effort is distributed throughout the Channel, with concentration in 27.7.E. The wind farm areas in 27.4.C appear to constrain fishing to the corridors between developments, potentially contributing to spatial concentration of effort in that division.

```{r gfw-plot-spatial-all, fig.height=6, fig.cap=fig_nums("gfw_events_all")}

events_sample <- events_classified_fr %>%

                               levels=c(report_countries_gfw, "Other"))) %>%
  slice_sample(n=sample_size) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords=c("lon","lat"), crs=4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs_proj) %>%
  mutate(x=st_coordinates(.)[,1], y=st_coordinates(.)[,2]) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  mutate(year = year(start))

ggplot() +
```

### Spatial distribution of fishing events by year

The annual maps reveal several notable patterns. Dutch (NLD) effort in 27.4.C shows progressive spatial compression over time, likely reflecting the expanding wind farm footprint pushing vessels into narrower corridors. French (FRA) effort in the Channel remains broadly stable in distribution throughout the series. UK (GBR) effort in 27.7.E appears to decline noticeably after 2020, consistent with post-Brexit fleet restructuring. From 2021 onwards, the spatial separation between national fleets becomes more pronounced, suggesting reduced overlap in fishing grounds following the EU-UK TCA access arrangements.
