### Kernel density in the study area

Kernel density estimation (KDE) converts the discrete set of fishing event locations into a continuous surface representing the spatial intensity of fishing effort. For each year, fishing event coordinates are projected into a metric coordinate system (UTM zone 30N) and a Gaussian kernel with bandwidth σ = `r sigma_all/1000` km is applied within the study area boundary (land excluded). The resulting density surface is normalised within each year to a 0–1 scale, where 1 represents the grid cell with the highest density and 0 the lowest. This within-year normalisation makes annual maps directly comparable in terms of spatial pattern but means that absolute effort levels cannot be compared between years, a year with low total effort and a year with high total effort will both have cells reaching 1.0. For absolute effort comparisons, refer to Figures `r fig_nums("gfw_flag_total", display="num")` and `r fig_nums("aer_gfw_compare", display="num")`.

The KDE maps corroborate and sharpen the patterns visible in the point distribution maps above. The persistent high-density hotspot in the southern North Sea (27.4.C) along the Dutch and Belgian coasts is clearly visible throughout the series, with the peak density area appearing to shift and compress progressively eastward over time, consistent with the displacement effect of expanding wind farm developments. In the Channel, the eastern entrance to 27.7.D around the Pas de Calais consistently shows the highest effort density, reflecting the concentration of French bottom trawl activity in this area. A notable feature emerging from around 2021–2022 is the relative weakening of the 27.7.E density signal, particularly in the northern (UK) portion of the division, reinforcing the post-Brexit reduction in UK fleet activity suggested by the point maps. The KDE representation also makes clear that while the spatial footprint of fishing appears broadly stable across the series, the intensity within hotspot areas has increased relative to background effort levels; a pattern that will be quantified further by the concentration metrics in the following section.

```{r gfw-plot-kde, fig.height=10, fig.cap=fig_nums("kde_all")}
ggplot() +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_tile(data=kde_results, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=ndensity)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option="inferno", name="Relative\ndensity",
                       limits=c(0,1), breaks=c(0,0.5,1),
                       labels=c("Low","Mid","High"), na.value="transparent") +
  geom_sf(data=world_proj, fill="grey85", colour="grey60", linewidth=0.2) +
  geom_sf(data=fao_div_proj, fill=NA, colour="grey30", linewidth=0.4) +
  coord_sf(crs=crs_proj,
           xlim=st_bbox(study_window_proj)[c("xmin","xmax")],
           ylim=st_bbox(study_window_proj)[c("ymin","ymax")],
           expand=TRUE) +
  theme(axis.text=element_blank(), axis.ticks=element_blank(),
        axis.title=element_blank(), legend.position="bottom",
        strip.background=element_rect(fill="grey90"),
        strip.text=element_text(face="bold", colour="grey20")) +
  labs(title=paste0("GFW: Fishing effort density, all fleets (σ = ", sigma_all/1000, " km)"),
       subtitle="Normalised per year  —  Land excluded") +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol=3)
```

### Kernel density in ICES 27.7.D

The eastern Channel (ICES 27.7.D) is the division of primary interest for the flyshoot fishery and is examined in more detail using a finer kernel bandwidth of σ = `r sigma_7d/1000` km, which resolves spatial structure at a scale more appropriate for within-division analysis. The estimation window is restricted to 27.7.D, with internal waters excluded, and the density surface is again normalised within each year to a 0–1 scale to allow direct comparison of spatial patterns across years independently of changes in total effort.

The 27.7.D KDE maps reveal a persistent concentration of effort in the eastern portion of the division, centred on the Pas de Calais and the Baie de Seine. This hotspot is visible throughout the series and reflects the sustained intensity of French OTB activity in these historically important grounds. Effort in the western portion of 27.7.D is consistently lower, with UK effort progressively weakening from around 2021, reinforcing the pattern identified in the full-area maps.

```{r gfw-plot-kde-7d, fig.height=10, fig.cap=fig_nums("kde_7d")}
bbox_7d <- fao_div_proj |>
  filter(division == "27.7.D") |>
  st_bbox()

ggplot() +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_tile(data = kde_7d, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = ndensity)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option   = "inferno", name = "Relative\ndensity",
                       limits   = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1),
                       labels   = c("Low", "Mid", "High"),
                       na.value = "transparent") +
  geom_sf(data = world_proj,   fill = "grey85", colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = fao_div_proj, fill = NA,       colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  coord_sf(crs    = crs_proj,
           xlim   = bbox_7d[c("xmin", "xmax")],
           ylim   = bbox_7d[c("ymin", "ymax")],
           expand = TRUE) +
  theme(axis.text  = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "grey20")) +
  labs(title    = paste0("GFW: Fishing effort density ICES 27.7.D (σ = ",
                          sigma_7d/1000, " km)"),
       subtitle = "Normalised per year  —  Internal waters and land excluded") +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 3)

```

## GFW effort spatial concentration analyses in 27.7.D

Two complementary metrics are used to quantify the spatial concentration of fishing effort across the `r cell_size/1000` km × `r cell_size/1000` km grid cells covering ICES 27.7.D.

The **Gini coefficient** is a standard inequality measure borrowed from economics, adapted here to quantify the unevenness of effort across grid cells. It ranges from 0 to 1: a value of 0 means fishing effort is spread perfectly uniformly across all cells; a value of 1 means all effort is concentrated in a single cell. In practice, fishing effort is always somewhat concentrated. Values above 0.7 indicate strong spatial concentration in a small number of areas, while values below 0.5 suggest a relatively dispersed fleet. A rising Gini over time indicates that the fleet is progressively concentrating in fewer locations.

The **top-10% cell share** is a more intuitive companion metric: it asks what percentage of the total annual fishing events falls within the 10% of grid cells that were most intensively fished that year. If effort were uniform, this would be exactly 10%. In practice values of 40–70% are common in concentrated fisheries, meaning that a small fraction of the available sea area absorbs most of the fishing pressure. Together, the two metrics capture different aspects of spatial concentration: the Gini summarises the full distribution of effort, while the top-10% share focuses specifically on the most intensively exploited areas.

Both metrics indicate a moderate but meaningful increase in spatial concentration of fishing effort in ICES 27.7.D over the study period. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.53–0.57 in 2013–2016 to 0.60–0.66 in 2019–2025, suggesting progressive compression of effort into a smaller number of grid cells. The top-10% cell share tells a similar story: the proportion of total effort in the most-fished 10% of cells increased from around 34–40% in the early period to a peak of 50% in 2020, before partially stabilising at 41–44% in recent years. Together these metrics quantify what the KDE maps suggested qualitatively: while the broad spatial footprint of fishing in the eastern Channel has remained relatively stable, effort has become more concentrated within already-intensively-fished areas. The peak in concentration around 2019–2020 coincides with a period of significant fleet restructuring driven by post-Brexit access uncertainty and the COVID-19 pandemic. The partial relaxation of concentration since 2021 may reflect fleets settling into new access arrangements under the EU-UK TCA, though values remain consistently above the pre-2018 baseline.

```{r gfw-plot-concentration, fig.height=4, fig.cap=fig_nums("concentration")}
p_gini <- ggplot(concentration_7d, aes(x=year, y=gini)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_line(colour="#E15759", linewidth=1) + geom_point(colour="#E15759", size=3) +
  geom_text(aes(label=round(gini,2)), vjust=-0.8, size=2.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=study_years) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,1), labels=scales::number_format(accuracy=0.01)) +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=90, vjust=0.5)) +
  labs(x="", y="Gini coefficient", title="Gini coefficient")

p_top10 <- ggplot(concentration_7d, aes(x=year, y=top10_pct)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_line(colour="#4E79A7", linewidth=1) + geom_point(colour="#4E79A7", size=3) +
  geom_text(aes(label=paste0(round(top10_pct,0),"%")), vjust=-0.8, size=2.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=study_years) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,NA), expand=expansion(mult=c(0,0.15)),
                     labels=scales::percent_format(scale=1)) +
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=90, vjust=0.5)) +
  labs(x="", y="% of total effort", title="Top-10% cell share")

p_gini + p_top10 +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = paste0("GFW: Effort concentration ICES 27.7.D  —  ",
                      cell_size/1000, " km grid  —  All fleets"),
    subtitle = "Left: Gini coefficient (0=uniform, 1=fully concentrated). Right: % effort in top-10% cells.")

```

The per-country KDE maps for ICES 27.7.D confirm that French effort dominates this division throughout all three periods, accounting for approximately 69–74% of GFW fishing days. This also drives the increase in the Gini coefficient and the top-10% share. The UK fleet contributes around 15–17%, with a modest decline in the most recent period (2022–2025) consistent with post-Brexit access restructuring. Belgian and Dutch effort in 27.7.D is substantially lower in absolute terms. On the shared colour scale used in the figure below, these fleets appear dark not because of absence of fishing activity but because their effort density is an order of magnitude lower than the French fleet. The spatial patterns for the UK fleet show a broad distribution across the western portion of the division, while Dutch effort is more concentrated in the eastern Channel near the Pas de Calais.

```{r gfw-plot-kde-7d-country, fig.height=10, fig.width=6, fig.cap=fig_nums("kde_7d_country")}

kde_flags   <- c("FRA", "GBR", "NLD", "BEL")

# Define periods — labels and year ranges
kde_periods <- list(
  "2013\u20132018" = 2013:2018,
  "2019\u20132021" = 2019:2021,
  "2022\u20132025" = 2022:2025
)

# Filter events to 27.7.D and relevant flags, derive year
events_7d <- events_classified_fr |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(lubridate::year(start))) |>
  filter(division    == "27.7.D",
         vessel_flag %in% kde_flags,
         year        %in% unlist(kde_periods))

# Project to UTM30N
events_7d_sf <- events_7d |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(crs_proj)

# Compute KDE per period × flag — pool all years within each period
kde_7d_grid <- expand.grid(
    period = names(kde_periods),
    flag   = kde_flags,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ) |>
  purrr::pmap_dfr(function(period, flag) {
    yrs <- kde_periods[[period]]
    pts <- events_7d_sf |>
      filter(vessel_flag == flag,
             year        %in% yrs)
    if (nrow(pts) < 20) return(NULL)

    coords  <- st_coordinates(pts)
    ppp_obj <- spatstat.geom::ppp(
      x      = coords[, 1],
      y      = coords[, 2],
      window = study_owin
    )
    kde_raw <- spatstat.explore::density.ppp(
      ppp_obj,
      sigma    = sigma_7d,
      dimyx    = c(200, 200),
      positive = TRUE
    )
    as.data.frame(kde_raw) |>
      rename(density = value) |>
      mutate(period      = period,
             vessel_flag = flag)
  })

# Normalise within each period column (shared scale per period)
# so that relative country contributions are visible across rows
kde_7d_grid <- kde_7d_grid |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(ndensity = (density - min(density, na.rm = TRUE)) /
                   (max(density, na.rm = TRUE) - min(density, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(vessel_flag = factor(vessel_flag, levels = kde_flags),
         period      = factor(period,      levels = names(kde_periods)))

# Crop to 27.7.D bounding box
bbox_7d <- fao_div_proj |>
  filter(division == "27.7.D") |>
  st_bbox()

ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = kde_7d_grid,
            aes(x = x, y = y, fill = ndensity)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option   = "inferno",
    name     = "Relative density",
    limits   = c(0, 1),
    breaks   = c(0, 0.5, 1),
    labels   = c("Low", "Mid", "High"),
    na.value = "transparent"
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = world_proj,   fill = "grey85",
          colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = fao_div_proj, fill = NA,
          colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  coord_sf(crs    = crs_proj,
           xlim   = bbox_7d[c("xmin", "xmax")],
           ylim   = bbox_7d[c("ymin", "ymax")],
           expand = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(period ~ vessel_flag) +
  labs(
    title    = paste0("GFW: Fishing effort density ICES 27.7.D by country and period",
                      " (\u03c3 = ", sigma_7d / 1000, " km)"),
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Periods: ", paste(names(kde_periods), collapse = ", "),
      "  \u2014  Density normalised within each period\n",
      "Colour scale is shared across countries within each period,",
      " reflecting relative fleet contributions"
    )
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text        = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks       = element_blank(),
        axis.title       = element_blank(),
        legend.position  = "bottom",
        legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"),
        strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9))
```

### Limitations of effort-based concentration metrics

The spatial concentration metrics presented above are based on GFW fishing event counts, which approximate the number of vessel-days in each grid cell. This is a measure of effort intensity in time. It does not account for the area of seabed swept per fishing event. That area varies considerably between gear types and is an important dimension of fishing impact that vessel-day counts alone cannot reveal. In addition, the increase in AIS coverage may impact on the spatial concentration metrics.

These limitations are particularly relevant for ICES 27.7.D. The FDI gear split in Section `r sec["split"]` shows a growing contribution of flyshoot (SSC/SDN) relative to conventional otter trawl (OTB) over the `r aer_split_years_start`–`r aer_years_end` period. These two gear types have very different relationships between fishing time and seabed area contacted.

Eigaard et al. (2017) estimated trawling intensity at both surface and subsurface levels from VMS and logbook data across European waters. They found that subsurface trawling intensities are generally much lower than surface intensities. The exception is beam trawl and dredge fisheries, where surface and subsurface contact areas are approximately equal because the heavy gear penetrates the sediment consistently across the full gear width. The Channel and southern North Sea show relatively high subsurface footprints largely for this reason.

For flyshoot, the relationship between surface and subsurface disturbance is different. The surface footprint is large while the subsurface disturbance is relatively low. Long ropes are deployed and retrieved across a wide area of seabed during the encircling phase of each set. The net footrope itself contacts a considerably smaller area with limited sediment penetration. A simple comparison of vessel-days between flyshoot and otter trawl therefore understates the surface seabed area contacted per vessel-day by flyshoot, while overstating its subsurface impact relative to beam trawl.

## Channel fisheries context: literature review

This section places the quantitative results from Sections `r sec["landings"]`–`r sec["conc"]` in the broader context of the Channel fisheries literature and southern North Sea. It draws on ICES WGCSE, STECF, Ifremer, MMO and peer-reviewed sources (see Section `r sec["lit_methods"]` for the literature selection approach).

### Fleet composition and dominant gear types

The Channel (ICES 27.7.d/e) supports one of the most diverse and intensively fished areas in Europe. The French fleet dominates total effort in the eastern Channel, contributing over 60% of total AER fishing days in most years (ICES, 2025a; Ifremer, 2026), consistent with the AER results in `r fig_nums("effort_gear_cat", display="cite")`, which show France as the largest contributor across all gear categories. Bottom trawl/seine gears account for the largest share of demersal fishing effort, targeting mixed assemblages of flatfish, cephalopods and small pelagics. The Dutch flyshoot fleet expanded through the 2010s (Quirijns et al., 2020), a trend visible in the AER and GFW series (Figures `r fig_nums("split_fra_nld", display="num")` and `r fig_nums("gfw_flag_total", display="num")`). Belgian beam trawl effort has declined substantially since the mid-2000s under pressure from fuel costs and quota restrictions (Departement Landbouw en Visserij, 2022), consistent with the low and declining Belgian effort in beam trawl panels throughout the AER figures.

The scallop dredge fishery is concentrated in the Baie de Seine (27.7.d) and western Channel (27.7.e), dominated by the French fleet with seasonal UK participation. Scallop landings from the Baie de Seine reached a record ~48,000 t in 2024–2025 (Ifremer, 2025). MSC certification has been granted for the Baie de Saint-Brieuc fishery (2022) and the Baie de Seine fishery (November 2024), covering the majority of French Channel scallop production (MSC, 2024). The AER landings data (Figures `r fig_nums("landings_top20", display="num")`, `r fig_nums("landings_spp_cty", display="num")` and `r fig_nums("landings_spp_gear", display="num")`) confirm scallops as one of the highest-tonnage species in the study area, dominated by the French dredge fleet.

Pot and trap fisheries targeting whelk (*Buccinum undatum*), crab and lobster are important to UK coastal communities, though the AER series shows limited representation of this segment at the fleet level. The whelk fishery in 27.7.d has grown markedly since the mid-2010s, driven by Asian export demand (MMO, 2023).

### Historical effort trends and structural change

Total fishing effort in the Channel has declined substantially since the early 2000s, consistent with EU fleet capacity reduction programmes and quota restrictions under successive CFP reforms. The AER series (`r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`) shows a general downward trend in fishing days for bottom trawl/seine and beam trawl across all major countries (`r fig_nums("effort_gear_cat", display="cite")`), with the Dutch flyshoot fleet being an important exception showing growth through the 2010s before stabilising post-2020. This is consistent with Quirijns et al. (2020) and STECF (2024).

Post-Brexit disruption from 2021 onwards has reshaped fleet access in the eastern Channel. UK licensing restrictions have reduced French, Belgian and Dutch access to UK waters in 27.7.d/e, driving spatial redistribution towards French EEZ waters (Phillipson & Symes, 2018; House of Lords, 2022). This structural shift may contribute to the apparent changes in spatial effort patterns visible in the GFW KDE maps (Figures `r fig_nums("kde_all", display="num")`–`r fig_nums("kde_7d", display="num")`) around 2021–2022, with effort concentrating in the southern (French EEZ) portion of 27.7.d. Post-Brexit bilateral agreements and access negotiations between the EU member states and the UK continue to shape fleet access patterns in the Channel.

The GFW spatial concentration metrics (`r fig_nums("concentration", display="cite")`) quantify whether this redistribution has led to concentrated effort patterns over time. An increase in Gini coefficient and top-10% share after 2021 is consistent with effort being pushed into a narrower range of spatial locations following access restrictions.

### Stock status of key target species

`r tab_nums("stock_status", display="cite")` summarises the assessment and advice status for the principal commercial stocks in the study area. Stocks are grouped by the ICES working group responsible for their assessment. Note that several species caught in the Channel, particularly cephalopods, do not have formal ICES assessments or TAC-based management; these are indicated accordingly.

```{r stock-status-table, echo=FALSE}
stock_status <- readxl::read_excel(
  file.path(r"(C:\Users\MartinPastoors\Martin Pastoors\FLYSHOOT - General\literature)", "stock_status.xlsx"),
  sheet = "Stock status"
)

# Colour coding of the status columns (6 = F vs FMSY, 7 = SSB vs Bpa):
#   F below FMSY = green, F above FMSY = red;
#   SSB above Bpa = green, SSB below or around Bpa = yellow, SSB at or below Blim = red
f_txt   <- coalesce(as.character(stock_status[[6]]), "")
ssb_txt <- coalesce(as.character(stock_status[[7]]), "")

f_green    <- which(str_detect(f_txt, "<"))
f_red      <- which(str_detect(f_txt, ">"))
ssb_red    <- which(str_detect(ssb_txt, "Blim"))
ssb_green  <- setdiff(which(str_detect(ssb_txt, ">")), ssb_red)
ssb_yellow <- setdiff(which(str_detect(ssb_txt, "<|~")), ssb_red)

hl <- function(ft, i, j, colour) {
  if (length(i) == 0) return(ft)
  flextable::highlight(ft, i = i, j = j, color = colour)
}

stock_status |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::italic(j = 1, part = "body") |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = c(1, 2)) |>
  style_ft(font_size = 7, total_row = FALSE) |>
  hl(f_green,    6, "green") |>
  hl(f_red,      6, "red") |>
  hl(ssb_green,  7, "green") |>
  hl(ssb_yellow, 7, "yellow") |>
  hl(ssb_red,    7, "red") |>
  flextable::set_caption(caption = tab_nums("stock_status"))
```

### Fisheries for squid

Squid has emerged as an increasingly important non-quota target species in the Channel and southern North Sea, particularly for the Dutch flyshoot fleet. The Dutch fleet, initially the flyshooters and more recently otter trawlers and beam trawlers, has increasingly targeted squid during winter, driven by high profitability, the need for fleet diversification, and the absence of quota restrictions. While the common squid (*Loligo vulgaris*) was once restricted to the English Channel, it is now turning up in large numbers in the southern North Sea, with Dutch fishermen fishing intensively for this species over the past five years. Brunel et al. (2025) provide a comprehensive characterisation of the Dutch squid fishery, documenting the fleet composition, seasonal and spatial dynamics of effort and landings, bycatch species composition, and stock assessment approaches for both *Loligo vulgaris* and *L. forbesii* in the Channel and southern North Sea. The English Channel has the highest long-finned squid landings in the Northeast Atlantic, making squid one of the most valuable resources exploited by demersal fisheries in this area.

Cephalopods in the Channel and southern North Sea, principally *Loligo vulgaris*, *L. forbesii*, common cuttlefish (*Sepia officinalis*) and horned octopus (*Eledone cirrhosa*), differ fundamentally from conventional fish stocks in their population dynamics (Van de Pol et al., 2025). They are semelparous, have life cycles of approximately one year, grow extremely fast and show high natural mortality, meaning annual stock size is almost entirely determined by recruitment success rather than spawning stock size. Abundance can therefore fluctuate dramatically between years in ways that make conventional MSY-based management approaches largely unsuitable. Both *Loligo* species have expanded their distribution northward into the southern North Sea in recent decades as water temperatures have risen, and survey data confirm a clear increase in their abundance since the mid-2010s. Despite their growing commercial importance, cuttlefish and squid together represent a substantial share of the landings in the eastern Channel and southern North Sea, no formal stock assessments or TACs exist for any of these species. Van de Pol et al. (2025) conclude that cephalopods currently operate without the biological safeguards applied to quota species and recommend development of assessment methods for *L. vulgaris* and *S. officinalis*.

### Ecosystem effects and sustainability

The seabed disturbance footprint of the Channel fisheries has been studied in the context of broader European assessments. Eigaard et al. (2017) estimated trawling intensity at surface and subsurface levels from VMS and logbook data across European shelf waters. They found that the relatively high subsurface footprint in the southern North Sea, Irish Sea, Celtic Sea and the Channel is largely due to the trawling activities of beam trawl and dredge fisheries, which have similar surface and subsurface contact areas. For most other bottom trawl types, subsurface intensities are much lower than surface intensities because gear components penetrate the sediment only shallowly. This distinction between surface and subsurface disturbance is important for evaluating the relative ecological impact of different gear types operating in the Channel. Comparisons between gear types show that Danish seine (flyshoot) has a large surface footprint due to the ropes deployed during the encircling phase, but a considerably smaller subsurface footprint, while beam trawl has similar surface and subsurface contact areas due to the deep penetration of tickler chains and beam shoes (Depestele et al., 2016; Eigaard et al., 2016a,b).

Bycatch and discards in the Channel mixed fisheries remain a management concern under the EU landing obligation (in force since 2019), though exemptions for high-survival species and *de minimis* provisions have reduced the practical scope of the obligation for many fleets (ICES WGCSE, 2025a). The flyshoot fishery is generally considered to have moderate bycatch rates compared to other demersal gears, though species composition of the bycatch varies considerably with area and season (Quirijns et al., 2020).


# Discussion & Synthesis

## Effort trends and fleet position

An important caveat throughout the AER-based analyses is that the UK fleet is not included, as the UK ceased reporting to STECF following Brexit. UK landings for `r min(uk_years)`–`r max(uk_years)` were added from the MMO data (Section `r sec["uk_landings"]`), but no UK effort data were available. Based on GFW data, UK vessels contribute approximately 25–30% of total fishing days in the study area, meaning the AER substantially under-represents total fishing pressure. The Other/mixed AER gear category presents a further interpretive challenge: it combines Dutch and French pelagic trawlers with French scallop and seaweed fisheries, making fleet-specific trend analysis impossible without additional data sources.

Total (EU) fishing effort in the Channel and Southern North Sea (ICES 27.4.c/27.7.d/27.7.e) has declined substantially over the `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end` period covered by the AER series, with a reduction of approximately 30% across all gears and countries combined. This decline is consistent with the long-term trend of EU fleet capacity reduction under successive CFP reform cycles, and with the structural contraction of the Belgian and Dutch beam trawl segments visible in both landings and effort data. France dominates the total effort picture throughout, contributing around 80% of fishing days, and its otter trawl (OTB) fleet in the eastern Channel shows a steady but gradual decline over the period.

The Dutch fleet presents a contrasting trajectory: although small in absolute days relative to the French fleet, it has been relatively stable and seine-dominated, with the FDI gear split confirming that roughly 70% of Dutch bottom trawl/seine days in the study area are attributable to seine gears. This fleet segment is small in AER terms but possibly disproportionately visible in the GFW spatial data because of the high AIS coverage on the larger vessel segments.

Post-Brexit restructuring from 2021 onwards has had a measurable effect on spatial distribution. The GFW annual maps show a progressive reduction in effort in the UK part of 27.7.e, consistent with altered access conditions under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement (European Commission, 2021). The Dutch fleet in 27.4.C shows spatial compression that could at least partly be attributable to the ongoing expansion of offshore wind farm development zones, which are progressively reducing the navigable fishing area available to trawl and seine vessels (Quirijns et al., 2020).

The spatial concentration metrics in 27.7.D (Gini coefficient rising from 0.53–0.57 in 2013–2016 to 0.60–0.66 by 2019–2025, top-10% cell share peaking at 50% in 2020) are consistent with this redistribution of effort and support the interpretation in Section `r sec["hist"]` that post-Brexit access restrictions compressed effort into a narrower spatial footprint from 2018 onwards.

## Contribution of the UK fleet

The MMO data show that the UK and Channel Islands fleets are a substantial user of the study area, accounting for around `r uk_share_pct`% of total landings over `r min(combined_years)`–`r max(combined_years)`. Their fishery profile differs clearly from that of the EU fleets: UK landings are dominated by shellfish taken with pots and traps and dredges, whereas EU landings are dominated by pelagic fish, seaweeds, flatfish and scallops. An analysis based on the AER alone therefore not only underestimates total landings but also gives a biased picture of the species and gear composition of the fisheries in the study area. The UK data also show substantial demersal seine (flyshoot) landings in 27.7.d.

No UK effort data were available, so the relative fishing pressure of UK vessels cannot be expressed in fishing days. The GFW data suggest that UK vessels account for roughly 25–30% of AIS-derived fishing days, which is of the same order as their share of landings.

## Comparison of AER and GFW effort metrics

The AER and GFW series measure effort using fundamentally different methodologies: administrative logbook declarations versus AIS-derived vessel-day estimates. Therefore, they are not directly comparable in absolute terms. The GFW series shows an increasing trend from 53,000 to 90,000 days over `r gfw_years_start`–`r max(study_years)`, while the AER shows a declining trend over `r gfw_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`. These opposing directions are reconciled by three structural factors: improving AIS coverage over the early years of the GFW series inflates apparent growth; GFW includes the UK fleet (contributing ~25–30% of total days) which is absent from the AER series; and GFW captures large vessels with high AIS compliance most accurately, while the AER captures the full administrative fleet including small inshore vessels below the AIS carriage threshold.

The most useful role of the GFW data in this report is therefore not as an independent cross-check of absolute effort levels, but as a source of spatial resolution unavailable from the AER. The within-division distribution of effort, the identification of national fishing grounds, and the detection of temporal shifts in spatial patterns can be based on GFW data. Used in this complementary way, the two sources are mutually reinforcing: the AER provides the authoritative time series of effort and landings by fleet segment, while GFW provides the spatial context that the AER cannot. The FDI was retained for the methodologically important role of gear-code disaggregation of the AER bottom trawl/seine category, but its quality limitations (confidentiality suppression, EU-aggregated landings) precluded its use as a primary effort or landings source (STECF, 2025b).

## Compliance with management measures and bilateral agreements

Direct assessment of compliance with effort and gear management measures is beyond the scope of this report, which relies on aggregated AER and GFW data rather than vessel-level logbook or VMS records. However, the data presented allow some observations relevant to the monitoring context. The GFW spatial concentration metrics in 27.7.D show an increase in Gini coefficient and top-10% cell share from 2018–2020 onwards, which coincides with the period of increasing negotiation pressure around Brexit access arrangements. This pattern is consistent with a progressive restriction of vessel access to previously used grounds, whether through formal licensing or informal avoidance. The partial reduction in effort concentration since 2022 may reflect stabilisation of access arrangements under the TCA, though concentration remains structurally elevated above pre-2018 levels.

The FDI gear split confirms that the Dutch fleet's contribution to bottom trawl/seine effort in the Channel is predominantly seine (flyshoot), providing a quantitative baseline against which future changes in gear composition could be assessed. It is noted that, as discussed in Sections `r sec["conc_limits"]` and `r sec["ecosystem"]`, flyshoot has a substantially larger surface footprint per vessel-day than otter trawl, even though its subsurface penetration is lower (Eigaard et al., 2016a,b; 2017). Therefore, the decline in (French) OTB fishing days does not automatically mean that the overall fishing pressure of the combined bottom trawl/seine category goes down with the same magnitude. As the share of flyshoot increases within the declining bottom trawl/seine category, the surface footprint per vessel-day may be growing even if total fishing days decline. This is an effect that vessel-day metrics alone cannot capture. More granular vessel-level monitoring combining VMS tracks with gear-specific swept-area coefficients would be required to quantify this effect and would represent a natural extension of the spatial analysis framework developed in this report.

# Conclusions & Recommendations

## Conclusions

This report has characterised fishing effort, landings and spatial distribution in the English Channel and southern North Sea (ICES 27.4.c/27.7.d/27.7.e) over the period `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end` (AER), `r aer_split_years_start`–`r aer_years_end` (FDI), `r min(uk_years)`–`r max(uk_years)` (UK landings, MMO) and `r gfw_years_start`–`r max(study_years)` (GFW), integrating four complementary data sources.

Total fishing effort has declined by approximately 30% since `r aer_years_start`, driven primarily by contraction of French otter trawl and Belgian and Dutch beam trawl effort. France dominates total effort throughout, contributing around 80% of AER fishing days. The Dutch flyshoot fleet, while small in absolute days, is the dominant seine fleet in the area and has remained relatively stable. The effort trends refer to EU fleets only, as no UK effort data were available.

EU landings are dominated by pelagic species, flatfishes, scallops, shrimps and seaweeds. Flatfish landings have declined markedly, consistent with the deteriorating stock status of Channel sole and plaice (ICES, 2025a; ICES, 2025b). Scallop landings show an increasing trend since 2016, supported by record biomass in the Baie de Seine (Varenne & Foucher, 2025). UK and Channel Islands vessels accounted for around `r uk_share_pct`% of total landings in the study area over `r min(combined_years)`–`r max(combined_years)`, with a fishery profile centred on shellfish (whelk, scallops, cockles and crab) taken by pots and traps and dredges. Including the UK increases total landings by roughly 20% relative to the AER and shifts the overall species composition towards shellfish and crustaceans.

The FDI-based gear-code disaggregation confirms that approximately 85–90% of bottom trawl/seine days in the study area are conventional otter trawl (predominantly French OTB), with seine gears (predominantly Dutch SSC/SDN) accounting for the remainder. This baseline characterisation provides the quantitative foundation against which future fleet developments and the effects of access agreements can be assessed.

GFW spatial analysis reveals persistent fishing hotspots in the Pas de Calais and Baie de Seine, with Dutch effort in 27.4.C showing progressive spatial compression likely linked to wind farm expansion. Post-Brexit spatial restructuring is visible from 2021, with declining UK effort in 27.7.e and increased spatial separation between national fleets. Spatial concentration in 27.7.D, as measured by the Gini coefficient and top-10% cell share, has increased from a pre-2018 baseline and remains elevated, pointing to a structural rather than temporary shift in spatial behaviour.

The effort-based concentration metrics should be interpreted alongside the gear composition results: the decline in bottom trawl effort leads to a growing share of flyshoot (SSC/SDN) within the bottom trawl/seine category. This implies a larger surface seabed footprint per vessel-day, even if total fishing days for the bottom trawl/seine category is declining. Quantifying the area swept per vessel-day using gear-specific coefficients from the ICES VMS data product (Eigaard et al., 2016a,b; 2017) would provide a more ecologically meaningful measure of the fleet's spatial impact and is recommended as a priority next step.

## Recommendations

1.  **Obtain UK effort data.** The most important gap in this analysis is the absence of UK fishing effort. UK effort data (fishing days, days at sea and kW-days by year, division, gear and vessel length, 2008–2025) should be requested from the MMO, so that the UK fleet can be included in the effort trends and the pre-Brexit period can be covered.
2.  **Improve the gear split between otter trawl and seine.** The FDI-based split is limited by confidentiality suppression. Unsuppressed FDI data, or national logbook data by gear code, should be requested from the relevant Member States (in particular France and the Netherlands) to make the split of the AER bottom trawl/seine category more robust.
3.  **Update the series when new data become available.** The AER series should be extended to `r aer_years_end + 1` once French data are published, and the UK series once the MMO publishes `r max(uk_years) + 1` data.
4.  **Verify data anomalies.** The anomalous Dutch pelagic landings attributed to 27.4.c in 2012 should be verified with STECF and the national data provider.

# Annexes

## Annex A Data sources

| Dataset             | Source                | Period                                        | Role in this report                         |
|---------------------|-----------------------|-----------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| STECF AER           | STECF 25-07           | `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`         | Primary: effort trends, landings            |
| UK landings         | MMO                   | `r min(uk_years)`–`r max(uk_years)`           | UK & Channel Islands landings               |
| STECF FDI           | STECF 25-10           | `r aer_split_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`   | Gear split key for AER bottom trawl/seine   |
| GFW Vessel registry | GFW                   | `r gfw_years_start`–`r max(study_years)`      | Flag, gear type, GT                         |
| GFW Events API      | GFW API v3 (gfwr 3.0) | `r gfw_years_start`–`r max(study_years)`      | Spatial analysis only                       |
| ICES/FAO shapefiles | ICES/FAO              | —                                             | ICES division polygons                      |

## Annex B Supplementary tables

The tables below summarise the key data extracted from the STECF AER and FDI datasets for the study area (ICES 27.4.c/27.7.d/27.7.e), covering the period `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`. Values are rounded for presentation; totals may not sum exactly due to rounding. All weights in tonnes (live weight); effort in fishing days.

::: {custom-style="Hheading 3"}
Table B1. Total landed weight (t) by country and year; all gears
:::

```{r annex-b1, echo=FALSE}
make_annex_table(
  df         = aer_landings_summary |>
                 filter(sub_reg %in% study_divisions_aer,          # no country filter here
                        year    %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end),
  row_var    = "year",     col_var   = "country_code",
  value_var  = "live_weight_t",
  row_label  = "Year",    col_levels = report_countries_aer,       # helper lumps the rest
  add_other  = TRUE
)

```

::: {custom-style="Hheading 3"}
Table B2. Total landed weight (t) by country and year for selected gears
:::

Selected gears: `r paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")`. ICES 4.c/7.d/7.e (AER, `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`).

```{r annex-b2, echo=FALSE}
make_annex_table(
  df         = aer_landings_summary |>
                 filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
                        gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
                        year          %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end),
  row_var    = "year",  col_var   = "country_code",
  value_var  = "live_weight_t",
  row_label  = "Year",  col_levels = report_countries_aer,
  add_other  = TRUE
)
```

::: {custom-style="Hheading 3"}
Table B3. Total landed weight (t) by species group and year for selected gears
:::

Selected gears: `r paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")`. Species groups as defined in Section `r sec["spp"]`. ICES 4.c/7.d/7.e (AER, `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`).

```{r annex-b3, echo=FALSE}
aer_landings_summary |>
  filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer) |>
  filter(gear_category %in% capacity_gears) |>
  filter(year          %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end) |>
  mutate(species_group = assign_species_group(species_code, species_name),
         species_group = if_else(is.na(species_group), "Other", species_group)) |>
  # filter(species_group=="Other") %>% 
  # filter(species_code=="SPR") %>% 
  # group_by(gear_category, species_code, species_name) %>% 
  # summarise(live_weight_t=sum(live_weight_t)) %>% 
  # arrange(desc(live_weight_t)) %>% 
  # View()

  make_annex_table(
    row_var    = "year",  col_var   = "species_group",
    value_var  = "live_weight_t",
    row_label  = "Year",  col_levels = c(species_group_levels, "Other"),
    add_other  = FALSE   # already recoded above
  )
```

::: {custom-style="Hheading 3"}
Table B4. Total fishing days by country and year for selected gears
:::

Selected gears: `r paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")`. ICES 4.c/7.d/7.e (AER, `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`).

```{r annex-b4, echo=FALSE}
make_annex_table(
  df         = aer_effort_summary |>
                 filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
                        gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
                        year          %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end),
  row_var    = "year",  col_var   = "country_code",
  value_var  = "totfishdays",
  row_label  = "Year",  col_levels = report_countries_aer,
  add_other  = TRUE
)
```

::: {custom-style="Hheading 3"}
Table B5. Total fishing days by vessel length class and year for selected gears
:::

Selected gears: `r paste(capacity_gears, collapse=", ")`. ICES 4.c/7.d/7.e (AER, `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`).

```{r annex-b5, echo=FALSE}
make_annex_table(
  df         = aer_effort_summary |>
                 filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
                        gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
                        year          %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end,
                        !vessel_length %in% c("UNKNOWN","NK")),
  row_var    = "year",  col_var   = "vessel_length",
  value_var  = "totfishdays",
  row_label  = "Year",
  col_levels = c("VL0010","VL1012","VL1218","VL1824","VL2440","VL40XX"),
  add_other  = TRUE
)
```

::: {custom-style="Hheading 3"}
Table B6. FDI gear split: fishing days by year and gear type (bottom trawl/seine only)
:::

Based on the FDI-derived disaggregation of the AER Bottom trawl/seine category. Only direct FDI splits are shown; pooled fallback and unsplit strata are excluded. See Section `r sec["fdi"]` for methodology.

```{r annex-b6, echo=FALSE}
if (!is.null(aer_split)) {
  make_annex_table(
    df         = aer_split |>
                   filter(split_source == "FDI direct",
                          year         %in% aer_years_start:aer_years_end),
    row_var    = "year",  col_var   = "gear_type",
    value_var  = "totfishdays_split",
    row_label  = "Year",
    col_levels = c("Bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB)", "Seine (SSC/SDN)"),
    add_other  = TRUE
  )
} else {
  cat("aer_split not available.\n")
}
```

::: {custom-style="Hheading 3"}
Table B7. Total fishing days by gear and year; focused gears with bottom trawl/seine split
:::

Bottom trawl/seine disaggregated into bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB) and seine (SSC/SDN) using FDI split key from `r aer_split_years_start` onwards. Other focused gears shown as reported in AER. '--' indicates gear not separately reported for that year. ICES 4.c/7.d/7.e (AER + FDI, `r aer_years_start`–`r aer_years_end`).

```{r annex-b7, echo=FALSE}
gear_order <- c("Bottom trawl/seine (unsplit)",
                "Bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB)",
                "Seine (SSC/SDN)",
                setdiff(capacity_gears, "Bottom trawl/seine"))

# Block 1: pre-2013 — BTS unsplit, other gears normal
pre2013_bts <- aer_effort_summary |>
  filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category == "Bottom trawl/seine",
         year          %in% aer_years_start:2012) |>
  group_by(year, gear_category) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  rename(gear_label = gear_category) |>
  mutate(gear_label = "Bottom trawl/seine (unsplit)")

pre2013_other <- aer_effort_summary |>
  filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
         gear_category != "Bottom trawl/seine",
         year          %in% aer_years_start:2012) |>
  group_by(year, gear_category) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  rename(gear_label = gear_category)

# Block 2: 2013+ — BTS split via FDI, other gears normal
post2013_bts <- if (!is.null(aer_split)) {
  aer_split |>
    filter(year      %in% 2013:aer_years_end,
           gear_type != "Unsplit") |>
    group_by(year, gear_type) |>
    summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays_split, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
    rename(gear_label = gear_type)
} else {
  aer_effort_summary |>
    filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
           gear_category == "Bottom trawl/seine",
           year          %in% 2013:aer_years_end) |>
    group_by(year, gear_category) |>
    summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
    rename(gear_label = gear_category) |>
    mutate(gear_label = "Bottom trawl/seine (unsplit)")
}

post2013_other <- aer_effort_summary |>
  filter(sub_reg       %in% study_divisions_aer,
         gear_category %in% capacity_gears,
         gear_category != "Bottom trawl/seine",
         year          %in% 2013:aer_years_end) |>
  group_by(year, gear_category) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  rename(gear_label = gear_category)

all_data <- bind_rows(pre2013_bts, pre2013_other,
                      post2013_bts, post2013_other) |>
  mutate(totfishdays = round(totfishdays)) |>
  group_by(year, gear_label) |>
  summarise(totfishdays = sum(totfishdays, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from  = gear_label,
              values_from = totfishdays,
              values_fill = NA) |>
  dplyr::select(year, any_of(gear_order)) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(any_of(gear_order)), na.rm=TRUE))

# Build total row separately on the completed data frame
total_row <- all_data |>
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) sum(x, na.rm=TRUE))) |>
  mutate(year = NA_integer_)

# Bind and convert year to character
all_data <- bind_rows(all_data, total_row) |>
  mutate(year = if_else(is.na(year), "Total", as.character(year)))

# Convert NA to "--" for display (must be character columns)
all_data_display <- all_data |>
  mutate(across(any_of(gear_order),
                \(x) if_else(is.na(x), "--", formatC(x, format="d", big.mark=","))))

# Rename year column
names(all_data_display)[1] <- "Year"

# Build flextable
ft <- flextable::flextable(all_data_display) |>
  style_ft(font_size = 8) |>
  # Right-align numeric-looking columns (all except Year)
  flextable::align(j = -1, align = "right", part = "all") |>
  flextable::align(j = 1,  align = "left",  part = "all") |>
  # Shade pre-2013 rows slightly to signal unsplit period
  flextable::bg(i = ~ Year %in% as.character(aer_years_start:2012),
                j = c("Bottom trawl (OTB/OTT/PTB)", "Seine (SSC/SDN)"),
                bg = "#EEEEEE")

ft
```
